newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe seeks confidence vote, faces fresh criticism.
newsitem.headline: Juppe seeks confidence vote, faces fresh criticism.

text.p: French Prime Minister Alain Juppe sought to unite his fractious centre-right coalition on Tuesday by calling a parliamentary vote of confidence in his economic policies for next week.

But the Gaullist premier faced fresh criticism from his junior government partners in the Union for French Democracy (UDF) over his proposals to change the electoral system and introduce tougher legislation against racism.

"To renew the contract that unites us for this legislature, especially in the eyes of the French public, I will seek a confidence vote in the National Assembly after a policy statement at the start of the new session," Juppe told UDF parliamentarians meeting in this chic Normandy beach resort.
Parliament reconvenes after the summer recess next Tuesday. Since the coalition holds four-fifths of the 577 assembly seats, the outcome of the vote is a foregone conclusion.

Juppe's move appeared aimed at outflanking critics of austerity in his own ranks, led by former Gaullist interior minister Charles Pasqua, a leading opponent of a single European currency, and outspoken UDF free-marketeer Alain Madelin.
Several coalition politicians have criticised planned income tax cuts as inadequate and sought a change in economic policy to boost sluggish growth and combat 12.5 percent unemployment.
By calling a confidence motion, Juppe was effectively challenging his critics to put up or shut up.

"Our mortal enemy is division and dissent...The antidote to division and dissent is unity," he declared, although in an effort to sound conciliatory, he said he was open to improvements in the draft 1997 budget.
After Juppe had left, UDF leader Francois Leotard lashed out at his suggestion of introducing "a dose" of proportional representation for the 1998 parliamentary elections.

The idea smacked of "a panicky government trying to save its skin by changing the rules of the game", Leotard said. The UDF had never requested such a change, nor would it happen without the party's support, he said.
Leotard derided the premier's attempts to draw centrists previously allied with the Socialists into his coalition.
He also criticised a draft anti-racism bill meant to make it easier to prosecute far-right National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen for espousing racial inequality.
"You can't legislate against stupidity...Existing legal weapons seem to me sufficient," Leotard said. "I don't think adding a specially tailored law would be appropriate."
The confidence debate comes as Juppe and President Jacques Chirac slumped back close to the record unpopularity they reached during last year's labour unrest.
A BVA opinion poll on Wednesday showed public approval of Chirac had fallen by six points to 46 percent in September and Juppe's rating stood at a mere 31 percent, down six points.
Socialist opposition floor leader Laurent Fabius compared Juppe's government to the orchestra continuing to play aboard the Titanic as the cruise liner hit an iceberg and sank.
"The country's economic situation is calamitous. It's easy to understand why the French people are gloomy," Fabius told Socialist parliamentarians meeting in Figeac.
"Regardless of the economic and social results, the government orchestra goes on playing on the Titanic," he said.
Juppe dismissed talk of a recession prompted by a recent slowdown and stressed he would stick to the goal of European monetary union.

"To give up now when we are so close to the goal would not only be regrettable, pathetic. It would be an error with heavy consequences, wasting the efforts made by the entire nation for several years, by our companies and our citizens," he said.
Juppe sought to cheer UDF deputies by promising to bring forward a bill this autumn to fight the use of illegal labour, a problem widely associated with illegal immigration.
